preamble: Vowel deletion, specifically the loss of the close back rounded vowel /u/, is a common phonetic transformation known as apocope (word-final deletion) or syncope (word-medial deletion). This process often occurs in unstressed syllables, contributing to syllable reduction and changes in word structure. In Trinitario Mojeño (Arawakan, Bolivia), rhythmic syncope deleted *u in weak and unfooted syllables.

examples.note: The unstressed final *-u was lost after a heavy syllable.
The final *-uz was lost, leaving u-umlaut of the root vowel.
Syncope of the unstressed post-tonic u, condemned in the Appendix Probi ('oculus non oclus'); cf. Italian occhio, maschio.
Word-final vowels of the proto-forms are lost.

examples.from: Kayardild yalulu 'flame, light' (keeps the final vowel)
examples.note: Lardil drops final short vowels in words of three or more morae.
In four-syllable words the vowels of the first and third syllables were lost: the weak member of the iambic foot and the unfooted syllable.

sources: Carvalho, F. O. de, & Rose, F. (2018). Comparative reconstruction of Proto-Mojeño and the phonological diversification of Mojeño dialects. LIAMES, 18(1), 3–44. https://doi.org/10.20396/liames.v1i1.8648804
